explanation_text: When France defined the metre, it was split into 10 decimetres, 100 centimetres, and 1000 millimetres, so each digit's position in a measurement tells its size. The 2 in 200 centimetres stands for hundreds, while the same 2 in 20 centimetres stands for tens—exactly how a digit's place gives a number its value.
image_prompt: A metre stick marked in decimetres, centimetres, and millimetres with positions labelled ones, tens, and hundreds, beside a French Revolutionary-era engraving of the metre standard.

french_culture: The changing level of the Seine
explanation_text: The Seine's water level rises when rains add water and falls in dry months when water is carried away. Adding rainfall raises the level and subtracting evaporation lowers it—the same combining and taking away you use when you add and subtract numbers.
image_prompt: A Paris riverside quay with two water gauges on the Seine, one labelled rain adds water with a plus sign and one labelled dry season removes water with a minus sign.

french_culture: Rows of vines in a vineyard
explanation_text: A vineyard is planted in neat rows of vines, so counting a whole field means multiplying the number of rows by the vines in each row. Dividing the picked grapes equally among the harvest barrels is division—splitting a total into equal groups.
image_prompt: Rows of grapevines stretching across a French vineyard with vines counted per row, and wooden barrels being filled with equal portions of grapes.

explanation_text: Pétanque is usually played with two players side by side on each team. When every player has a partner, the count is even; if one player stands alone with no partner, that leftover makes the count odd.
image_prompt: A pétanque court in Provence with players paired up in twos, and one single player standing alone marked as the odd one out.

french_culture: Threads counted on a Gobelins loom
explanation_text: Weavers at the Gobelins factory count warp threads in rhythmical groups as they set up a tapestry. Counting threads 5 at a time or 10 at a time is skip counting, the same quick counting used to build number patterns.
image_prompt: A weaver at a large Gobelins loom pointing at bundles of warp threads, each bundle of five threads marked, showing skip counting by 5s and 10s.

explanation_text: A boulangerie posts each bread's price: a baguette at 1.10 euros, a country loaf at 1.50 euros. Comparing the tags shows which price is greater and which is less, just as you compare numbers by their digits.
image_prompt: A Paris boulangerie display of breads with price tags in euros, with a greater-than symbol drawn between a 1.10 tag and a 1.50 tag.

explanation_text: Bakers price breads using the old 1-2-3-4 rule so most prices end in a 9 or a 0, like 0.99 or 1.00 euro. Rounding each price to a convenient amount lets a shopper estimate the total of a basket before reaching the till.
image_prompt: A hand-written price board in a French boulangerie showing prices like 0.99 and 1.00 euros, with arrows showing how amounts round to the nearest convenient price.

explanation_text: A round camembert is cut into equal wedges, and each wedge is one part of the whole wheel. One wedge out of eight is the fraction 1/8, where the numerator counts the wedges and the denominator counts the equal parts of the wheel.
image_prompt: A whole camembert cheese wheel beside the same wheel cut into eight equal wedges, one wedge highlighted and labelled 1/8.

french_culture: Folding a crêpe in halves and quarters
explanation_text: Fold a crêpe once and you have two equal parts; fold it twice and you get four equal parts. The amount of crêpe is still the same, so 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions—different names for the same portion.
image_prompt: A stack of crêpes with one folded into a half and another folded twice into quarters, both labelled with the equivalent fractions 1/2 and 2/4.

french_culture: Slices of a galette des rois
explanation_text: A galette des rois is cut into eight equal slices for sharing. Grouping four slices gives half of the cake, so 4/8 simplifies to 1/2 by dividing the top and bottom by the same number.
image_prompt: A golden galette des rois cut into eight slices, with four slices grouped together and labelled 4/8 equals 1/2.

french_culture: Full and half litre bottles of milk
explanation_text: A shopper at the market carries two full litre bottles of milk and one bottle that is only half full. That total is 2 whole litres plus half a litre, written 2 1/2—a mixed number with a whole part and a fraction.
image_prompt: Two full litre milk bottles and one half-full bottle arranged on a market table, labelled 2 1/2 litres.

explanation_text: If a cheese plate holds five quarter-wheels of camembert, that is five parts where four make one whole wheel. Because 5/4 is more than one whole, it is called an improper fraction—the numerator is larger than the denominator.
image_prompt: A cheese plate with five quarter-wheels of camembert, four quarters forming one full circle and the extra quarter beside them, labelled 5/4.

explanation_text: At a fromagerie, two quarter-wheels of comté are brought together on the board. Adding fractions means combining same-sized parts, so 1/4 plus 1/4 equals 2/4, which is half of the wheel.
image_prompt: Two quarter-wheels of comté cheese being slid together on a wooden board to form a half circle, labelled 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

explanation_text: A glass of citron pressé is full, then a quarter of it is poured out to leave three quarters. Removing one fractional part from a whole shows fraction subtraction: 1 minus 1/4 equals 3/4.
image_prompt: A glass of pale yellow citron pressé on a café table, with a quarter of the glass marked as poured out and the remaining 3/4 shaded.

french_culture: Half of half a tarte aux pommes
explanation_text: Cut a slice of tarte aux pommes in half and you take half of that slice. Taking half of a half finds 1/2 of 1/2, which is 1/4—multiplying fractions means finding a part of a part.
image_prompt: A slice of apple tarte on a plate cut in half, with one quarter shaded and labelled 1/2 of 1/2 equals 1/4.

french_culture: Quarters cut from a folded crêpe
explanation_text: A crêpe folded and cut into quarters gives four equal pieces. Asking how many quarter-crêpes fit into a half-crêpe shows fraction division: 1/2 divided by 1/4 equals 2.
image_prompt: A folded crêpe on a plate cut into quarters, with two quarters grouped inside a half-circle outline, labelled 1/2 divided by 1/4 equals 2.

explanation_text: A café menu prices a pain au chocolat at 1.50 euros, where the digits after the decimal point stand for centimes. The decimal point separates whole euros from centimes, just as it separates whole numbers from tenths and hundredths.
image_prompt: A French café menu board showing prices such as 1.50 and 2.75 euros, with the decimal points highlighted and centimes marked as parts of a euro.

french_culture: Half a litre in a measuring jug
explanation_text: A metric measuring jug marks the same amount both as 1/2 litre and as 0.5 litre. Because the metric system is decimal, every simple fraction has a clean decimal twin, so converting 1/2 to 0.5 is a matter of place value.
image_prompt: A clear metric measuring jug in a kitchen with 1/2 litre and 0.5 litre marked at the same level, showing the two names for one amount.

explanation_text: French students are graded out of 20, so a score of 15 out of 20 means 15 of every 20 points. Because percent means per hundred, that score is converted to 75 out of 100, or 75 percent.
image_prompt: A French school report card with a grade of 15/20 next to an arrow showing it converted to 75%, with the words per cent explained as per hundred.

explanation_text: During the soldes, France's official January sales, a winter scarf marked 30 percent off asks you to find 30 percent of the original price. Finding a percent of a number means taking that part of the total, so 30 percent of 40 euros is 12 euros.
image_prompt: A shop window during the French January soldes with a red 30% off sign over a scarf price tag, showing the discount calculation 30% of 40 = 12 beneath.

explanation_text: A Vélib' bike-share station may hold some bikes, but you do not know how many until you count them. That unknown count can stand for a letter, x, just as an unknown quantity in math is called a variable.
image_prompt: A Paris Vélib' bike station with several bikes in the racks and a mystery number written as x floating above the empty spaces.

explanation_text: If 3 bikes are locked in a rack and x more riders are returning bikes, the total is written 3 + x. Putting known numbers and variables together like this forms an algebraic expression.
image_prompt: A Vélib' rack with 3 parked bikes and an empty slot marked x, with the expression 3 + x written beside it.

explanation_text: A pâtissier weighs flour on a two-pan balance: when both sides hold equal weight, the pans sit level. This balance of two equal amounts is exactly what an equation states, with both sides equal in value.
image_prompt: A brass balance scale in a French pâtisserie with equal bags of flour on both pans, the scale level and labelled equal weights, balanced equation.

explanation_text: A student already has 8 points on a test graded out of 20 and needs 12 to pass. Finding the missing points means solving x + 8 = 12 in one step, x = 4, by doing the opposite operation.
image_prompt: A French classroom scene with a test marked 8/20 so far, an empty box labelled x, and a pencil writing x + 8 = 12 with the answer 4.

explanation_text: A proper Savoyard fondue takes two steps: first grate the cheese, then melt it in the pot. Solving a two-step equation also needs two careful operations in order, undoing each step to find the unknown.
image_prompt: A Savoyard fondue scene with step one showing grated cheese and step two showing the melted pot, labelled like a two-step equation to solve.

explanation_text: On a mountain stage of the Tour de France, one rider may be 40 seconds ahead of another. The comparison ahead of is an inequality, written with a greater than or less than sign between the two times.
image_prompt: Two cyclists on a Tour de France mountain stage, one clearly ahead, with the inequality symbol shown between their split times on a roadside screen.

explanation_text: A pâtissier builds a mille-feuille in a fixed order: puff pastry, crème, pastry, crème, and powdered sugar on top. Doing the layers out of order ruins the cake, just as evaluating a math expression out of order gives the wrong answer.
image_prompt: A mille-feuille in cross-section showing its neat layers of pastry and cream, with numbered labels 1, 2, 3 showing the order they are stacked.

explanation_text: If a recipe asks for butter and the cook uses the same amount of margarine instead, one value has replaced another. Substituting a number for a variable in an expression is the same swap—replace the letter with its value.
image_prompt: A French kitchen with a recipe card showing butter, and a block of margarine of equal weight replacing it on the scale, labelled substitute the value.

explanation_text: Each thrown boule comes to rest at a single spot on the pétanque terrain. Like the point where the jack landed, every boule marks one exact location—the same idea as a point in geometry.
image_prompt: A pétanque terrain with steel boules scattered on the ground and small dots marking their landing spots, one dot labelled as a geometric point.

french_culture: Lines on the Paris Métro map
explanation_text: Each Métro line is drawn as a straight coloured line that runs on and on across the map. A geometric line is the same idea—a straight path with no end in either direction.
image_prompt: A Paris Métro map with straight coloured lines in every direction, several lines highlighted to show they continue beyond the edges.

explanation_text: The crisscrossing iron girders of the Eiffel Tower meet at countless sharp corners. Where two girders cross they form an angle, and the tower's strength comes from the exact size of these angles.
image_prompt: A close-up of the Eiffel Tower's iron lattice work with one crossing of girders highlighted and its angle measured with a protractor overlay.

french_culture: Beams meeting in the Eiffel Tower
explanation_text: Inside the Eiffel Tower, iron beams meet at clean right angles to brace the structure. Two lines meeting at a 90-degree angle are called perpendicular, and the tower depends on thousands of these right-angle joints.
image_prompt: An interior view of the Eiffel Tower's iron framework with two beams crossing at a right angle, a small 90-degree square drawn at the corner.

explanation_text: The two rails of a high-speed TGV track run side by side at a fixed distance, never meeting no matter how far they stretch. Lines that stay an equal distance apart forever are called parallel lines.
image_prompt: A TGV train rushing along straight tracks, with the two parallel rails receding into the distance and a dashed line showing the equal gap between them.

explanation_text: Seen from the palace windows, the parterre beds of Versailles are closed shapes with straight sides and corners. Any flat closed shape made of straight line segments is a polygon, from triangles to hexagons.
image_prompt: A bird's-eye view of the parterre gardens of Versailles with geometric boxwood beds forming triangles, squares, and hexagons.

french_culture: Glass panes of the Louvre pyramid
explanation_text: The glass panels of the Louvre's pyramid are all triangles that lean inward to meet at the point at the top. A triangle is a polygon with exactly three sides and three corners, and the pyramid's strength comes from them.
image_prompt: The glass pyramid of the Louvre at sunrise, with one triangular pane highlighted and its three sides and three vertices labelled.

explanation_text: The courtyards and windows of a Loire château are built as four-sided shapes with straight walls. Four-sided polygons such as rectangles, squares, and trapezoids are called quadrilaterals.
image_prompt: A Loire Valley château with its rectangular courtyard and rows of square window frames highlighted with four-sided outlines.

french_culture: Walking around the Place des Vosges
explanation_text: A walk all the way around the square Place des Vosges follows its boundary and returns to the start. The total distance around the outside of a shape is its perimeter.
image_prompt: The arcaded Place des Vosges in Paris seen from above, with a dashed red walking path tracing its four sides back to the starting point.

explanation_text: A lavender farmer measures how much of the field is covered by rows of lavender to know how much to harvest. The amount of surface a shape covers is its area, counted in squares like square metres.
image_prompt: Rows of purple lavender in a Provençal field with a grid of square metres drawn over the plants to show the area being covered.

explanation_text: In a French vineyard cellar, each barrique barrel holds a fixed amount of the harvest. The space inside a three-dimensional container, measured in litres, is its volume.
image_prompt: A stone wine cellar with rows of wooden barrique barrels, one barrel labelled with its capacity in litres and a measuring line at the fill level.

explanation_text: The rose window of Notre-Dame is a great circle of stained glass. Every line from the centre to the rim is a radius, twice a radius is the diameter, and the distance all the way around is the circumference.
image_prompt: The stained-glass rose window of Notre-Dame with a radius drawn from centre to edge, a diameter across, and the circumference traced around the rim.

explanation_text: Measure any round Brie wheel and its distance around is always a little more than three times its distance across. That fixed ratio, about 3.14, is the number pi.
image_prompt: A whole round Brie cheese wheel with a measuring tape around its edge and a line across its middle, labelled circumference and diameter with pi written at the centre.

french_culture: The grid of the Paris Métro
explanation_text: Métro lines cross at right angles like the axes of a graph, and every station sits where a line and a distance meet. A coordinate plane is the same grid, where each point is named by two numbers, x and y.
image_prompt: A Paris Métro map overlaid with a coordinate grid, one station highlighted and labelled with its x and y coordinates.

explanation_text: A visitor marks each château of the Loire valley on a map of the river's route. Placing each one at its correct spot is plotting points, just as you place points on a coordinate plane using ordered pairs.
image_prompt: A hand-drawn map of the Loire river with small icons marking Chambord, Chenonceau, and other châteaux, each pinned like a plotted point with coordinates.

french_culture: The parterre mirror garden of Versailles
explanation_text: In the formal gardens of Versailles, the pattern on one side of a central path is the mirror image of the other side. A design that folds perfectly onto its reflection has symmetry along a line.
image_prompt: A Versailles parterre garden divided by a central path, one half the mirror reflection of the other, with a dashed line down the middle.

explanation_text: Shops near the bay sell Mont-Saint-Michel as a small model in which every building is shrunk by the same factor. Shrinking or enlarging a shape while keeping its form is a dilation, one kind of geometric transformation.
image_prompt: A small wooden model of Mont-Saint-Michel sitting beside the real abbey on its island, with arrows showing the same shape at two different sizes.

explanation_text: A Breton recipe makes crêpe batter with 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of milk. Comparing the two amounts, 2 to 1, is a ratio that keeps every crêpe consistent.
image_prompt: A mixing bowl of pale crêpe batter beside two measuring cups, one of flour and one of milk, with the ratio 2:1 written between them.

explanation_text: To fit the rose window design on a wall chart, every part is enlarged by the same factor so the circle keeps its perfect roundness. Keeping ratios the same while changing size is maintaining proportion.
image_prompt: The design of the Notre-Dame rose window drawn small on paper and large on a wall, with grid lines showing every part scaled by the same factor.

french_culture: Average speed in the Tour de France
explanation_text: A rider covering 90 kilometres in 2 hours travels at an average of 45 kilometres per hour. Distance per single hour is a unit rate—how much of something happens for every one unit of time.
image_prompt: A Tour de France cyclist racing past a roadside sign showing 45 km per hour, with a small graph of distance against one hour of time.

french_culture: The Tour de France route map
explanation_text: The race programme prints the Tour's 3,400-kilometre route on a single page map. Because every part shrinks by the same ratio, the map is a scale drawing that keeps distances proportional.
image_prompt: A printed Tour de France route map with the scale legend 1 cm = 20 km, the race path drawn as a coloured line across France.

french_culture: Growing crowds at the Eiffel Tower
explanation_text: Monthly visitors to the Eiffel Tower rise from 100,000 to 120,000, an increase of 20,000. Since 20,000 is 20 percent of the starting 100,000, this is a 20 percent increase—a percent change.
image_prompt: Two panels showing the Eiffel Tower, one labelled 100,000 visitors and the next 120,000, with a rising arrow and +20% between them.

explanation_text: A baker records how many baguettes, pains au chocolat, and croissants are sold each day to know what to bake tomorrow. Writing down counts of each kind is data collection.
image_prompt: A boulangerie counter with baskets of bread and a handwritten ledger tallying baguettes and pastries sold, with tick marks beside each name.

explanation_text: The Métro timetable lists each station in order with the arrival time beside it. Arranging data in rows and columns this way is a table, the clearest way to read many values at a glance.
image_prompt: A Paris Métro timetable board listing station names in one column and arrival times in another, with a row highlighted.

explanation_text: A French student's report lists grades of 12, 15, and 18 in three subjects. Adding them and dividing by three gives an average of 15, which is the mean of the three grades.
image_prompt: A French report card with grades 12, 15, and 18, an addition line, and the average 15 circled at the bottom.

french_culture: Middle stage time in the Tour de France
explanation_text: The times of seven Tour de France finishers are arranged from fastest to slowest. The time exactly in the middle, with three faster and three slower, is the median.
image_prompt: A finish line screen listing seven rider times in order from fastest to slowest, with the middle time highlighted and labelled median.

explanation_text: On a village pétanque green, most of the boules are the classic dark steel colour. The value that appears most often in a group, like that colour, is called the mode.
image_prompt: A pile of pétanque boules, most of them dark steel with a few red and blue ones, the steel colour circled and labelled most frequent, the mode.

explanation_text: Between the same two cities, the quickest TGV journey takes 2 hours and the slowest takes 3 hours. Subtracting the fastest time from the slowest gives a spread of 1 hour, which is the range of the data.
image_prompt: A TGV platform display showing two train times for the same route, 2 hours and 3 hours, with a double-headed arrow between them labelled range equals 1 hour.

explanation_text: A sports page shows each Ligue 1 team as a bar whose height is its number of goals. Reading the bar heights lets you compare the teams at a glance, which is exactly what a bar graph is for.
image_prompt: A sports newspaper graph with coloured bars for Ligue 1 football teams and the number of goals beside each bar.

explanation_text: As the TGV speeds toward Lyon, its distance from Paris grows steadily with each hour. Drawing those distances over time as a rising line shows how a line graph displays a change as you read left to right.
image_prompt: A distance-versus-time line graph beside a TGV racing past the countryside, with hours on one axis and kilometres on the other.

explanation_text: A farmer's journal records that lavender, wheat, and vines each take their share of the fields. Showing those shares as slices of a circle makes a pie chart, where each slice shows a part of the whole.
image_prompt: A circular pie chart divided into purple, gold, and green slices labelled lavender, wheat, and vines, with a farm in Provence behind it.

french_culture: Finding the fève in a galette des rois
explanation_text: One tiny porcelain fève is hidden inside a galette des rois cut into eight equal slices. With one fève in eight slices, your chance of finding it is 1 in 8—an example of probability written as a fraction.
image_prompt: A galette des rois cut into eight slices on a golden plate, with a small porcelain fève peeking from one slice and 1 in 8 written above.

explanation_text: Gobelins weavers repeat the same flower-and-leaf motif again and again down the length of a tapestry. This predictable repetition of a motif is a pattern, just like a repeating number sequence.
image_prompt: A section of a Gobelins tapestry showing a flower-and-leaf motif repeated in a row, with one motif outlined and the repeats marked.

explanation_text: Along one Métro line, each stop number points to exactly one station name. A rule that gives each input exactly one output is a function, so the line's stops form a function from numbers to stations.
image_prompt: A straight Métro line diagram with stop numbers 1, 2, 3 each pointing by an arrow to a distinct station name, labelled input and output.
